raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a transcatheter strategy for reducing thromboembolism in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), based on the observation that most thrombi in nonvalvular AF arise from the left atrial appendage (LAA). The procedure typically uses femoral venous access, transseptal puncture, intraprocedural anticoagulation, fluoroscopy with transesophageal or intracardiac echocardiographic guidance, and deployment of an endocardial occluder at the LAA ostium. Its clinical appeal is greatest when lifelong oral anticoagulation (OAC) is hazardous, unacceptable, or impractical; however, LAAC is not a simple “anticoagulation substitute,” because it trades chronic pharmacologic bleeding risk for procedural risk, device-related thrombosis, residual leak, and the need for at least short-term postimplant antithrombotic therapy [1,2].

The foundational randomized evidence came from PROTECT AF, in which Watchman LAAC was noninferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death but had more early safety events [1,2]. PREVAIL showed improved procedural safety, although one coprimary efficacy criterion was not met in the setting of low event rates [3]. Longer-term pooled analyses of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL suggested comparable stroke prevention to warfarin, with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, disabling or fatal stroke, cardiovascular or unexplained death, all-cause death, and postprocedural bleeding [4,5]. For patients ineligible for warfarin, ASAP provided nonrandomized support for Watchman implantation with antiplatelet-based therapy [6], and EWOLUTION and the U.S. NCDR LAAO Registry confirmed high implant success and acceptable early outcomes in older, comorbid “real-world” cohorts [7,8]. One-year NCDR data showed low thromboembolic event rates despite high baseline risk, but mortality and bleeding reflected the frailty of treated populations [9].

Device design has evolved substantially. The Watchman FLX was developed to improve recapture, sealing, sizing range, and atraumatic deployment; PINNACLE FLX reported high closure success and low early safety-event rates [14]. The Amulet device, with a lobe-and-disc design, was compared with Watchman in Amulet IDE: Amulet was noninferior for safety and effectiveness and superior for anatomic occlusion, although early procedure-related complications were higher and improved with experience [15]. Three-year Amulet IDE outcomes showed durable clinical results [16]. SWISS-APERO, using CT-based assessment, found broadly similar early patency-related outcomes between Amulet and Watchman/FLX, with different trade-offs in leak and procedural complications [17].

The direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) era has refined the role of LAAC. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk patients to LAAC or DOACs and demonstrated noninferiority for a broad composite of ischemic, bleeding, and cardiovascular outcomes, with durable 4-year results favoring fewer clinically relevant bleeding events after the periprocedural phase [18,19]. OPTION extended the evidence to patients undergoing AF ablation, showing LAAC reduced nonprocedural bleeding and was noninferior to OAC for death, stroke, or systemic embolism at 36 months [20]. By contrast, CLOSURE-AF, in older patients at high stroke and bleeding risk, did not demonstrate noninferiority of LAAC versus physician-directed medical therapy [23]. CHAMPION-AF, a large contemporary trial in patients suitable for anticoagulation, found Watchman FLX noninferior to NOAC therapy for cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism and superior for nonprocedural bleeding at 3 years [24]. These mixed but complementary trials emphasize that benefit depends on baseline bleeding risk, competing mortality, procedural risk, and the comparator regimen.

Postimplant antithrombotic therapy remains unsettled. Registry analyses show wide variation in practice and suggest that avoiding aspirin when OAC is used may reduce early adverse events [10]. Small randomized data from ADALA suggest low-dose DOAC may reduce thromboembolism, device-related thrombus, or major bleeding compared with dual antiplatelet therapy after LAAC, with supportive 1-year follow-up [21,22]. Device-related thrombus occurs in a minority of patients but is clinically important; meta-analyses and registries link it to thromboembolic risk, support surveillance imaging, and usually prompt temporary anticoagulation when feasible [11-13]. Peridevice leak is another concern, especially when moderate or large, although definitions and imaging modalities vary.

Current expert documents and AF guidelines support percutaneous LAAC as reasonable in patients with AF, elevated stroke risk, and a nonreversible contraindication to long-term OAC, and as a possible alternative in selected patients at high bleeding risk after shared decision-making [26-28]. Imaging-based planning, experienced operators, careful transseptal technique, and structured follow-up are essential [29]. Future work should clarify optimal postimplant therapy, management of device-related thrombus and leak, comparative effectiveness versus lower-cost generic DOACs, outcomes in intracranial hemorrhage and advanced kidney disease, and whether first-line LAAC improves patient-centered outcomes beyond bleeding avoidance [25,30].
